title: Three Candidates
problem: Three candidates have distinct qualities and arrive in uniformly random order. You must accept or reject each immediately and cannot return. Consider the strategy: reject the first candidate, then accept the next candidate better than the first; if none is better, accept the last. What is the probability this strategy selects the best candidate?

hints.text: Enumerate the six relative arrival orders of best, middle, and worst.
The strategy succeeds when the first candidate is middle and best arrives second, or when the first is worst and best arrives second.

solution.setup: Represent arrival order using B, M, and W for best, middle, and worst.
solution.reasoning: Checking the six orders: BMW fails, BWM fails, MBW succeeds, MWB fails, WBM succeeds, and WMB succeeds because no one beats W until the last candidate B. Thus three of six orders succeed.
solution.sanityCheck: Rejecting the best first always loses, which occurs one-third of the time; the remaining success rate of one-half is plausible.

keyInsight: Optimal-stopping rules should be evaluated over relative ranks, not absolute candidate values.
recognitionCues: Sequential irreversible decisions in random order suggest conditioning on ranks and enumerating stopping outcomes.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that the last candidate is accepted when no earlier candidate clears the benchmark.
followUps: Is rejecting the first candidate optimal for three candidates?

verification.notes: Strategy succeeds on 3 of 6 relative orders.
